reason: A leaf sheath margin can be concave, and the examples describe the margin shape.
Fruit pulp can taste bitter, and the examples say so. A rule should read the taste of the pulp.
The examples give a diameter for cyathia, which is a sensible measurement.
Antheridia can sit at the tip of a shoot, so terminal position is meaningful.
'Structure' is a wrong reading. The examples say the crown is dense or leafy. That is density or foliage, not the structure quality.
Some examples are about cilia of the endostome, which is a different part. A rule would need to restrict this to real trichomes.
'Shrunken when dry' is a drying state of a fully developed leaf. PATO hypotrophic means underdeveloped, so the meaning is wrong.
The endostome surface can be smooth.
The presence of a hyalodermis in the stem epidermis is a normal presence statement.
'Many' is a count, not presence, and 'not differentiated' is an absence. A rule would need to separate presence, absence and quantity.
A capsule can be cup-shaped, and the examples are correct.
'Straight wet or dry' is a condition on the shape, not a wetness of the seta. The wetness reading is wrong.
'Perfect' here means a complete trellis of the endostome. The PATO term means hermaphrodite, so the reading is wrong.
Hyaline cell walls can be ornamented or not.
The examples mix fissuring with sulcate, and some may describe the whole petiole. A rule would need to map fissured and sulcate to surface-pattern terms.
A vein can be raised above or below the leaf surface.
A spathe can be thin.
A thallus surface can be smooth.
Achenes can be prism-shaped, and the examples are correct.
The examples describe the central column or the tube widening upward. The part is wrong, because the flower itself is not dilated.
'Solitary' or 'grouped' fits drupes borne singly or in groups, but one example is vein reticulation, which is a different quality. A rule would need to keep only solitary and grouped.
Stamens can be arranged on one side only.
A style can sit in the centre of the pistil.
Cotyledons can have an entire margin.
A pappus can form a ring (annular).
Thick describes the thickness of the part, and the examples are correct.
'Peu nombreuses' says there are few staminate flowers, not that the flower has fewer parts. The reading is wrong. Use a count or quantity of flowers on the plant.
The height of buttresses is a normal measurement.
Secondary veins can be thin.
A crown can be deep, and 'cime' here is the tree crown.
A thickness in mm is a normal measurement for lobes.
A lodicule (squamella) can be short.
'Velu' means hairy in general, not velvety. The velutinous reading is wrong. Use a hairy or pubescent term.
'Dressées' for veins is unclear. The basal ones may be lobes or veins that point upward. A rule would need to check what the term refers to.
The part can have wings, and the examples describe winged structures correctly.
Panicles can be borne singly (solitary).
An inflorescence axis can be angular.
A raceme can be elongated.
A width in mm is a normal measurement.
A bract can be asymmetric.
'Divisées en ramilles' says a branch divides into branchlets. That is branching, not a dissected shape. The PATO term is the wrong reading.
A stipule can be widened, for example at the base.
Domatia can be inconspicuous.
Cotyledons can be notched at the base.
The examples are probably about the position of something within the short shoot, such as the pith. The part is likely wrong.
Thickness of the part is a normal quality, and the examples are correct.
Lobes can be winged.
A connective appendage can have an obtuse apex.
An involucral bract surface can be smooth.
A fruit pedicel can be long, and the examples give lengths. A rule could map measurements to length instead.
An androphore can taper.
'Secondary roots' names a kind of root, not a quality of the root. The reading is wrong. Use the lateral root part instead.
Root nodules can be linear in shape.
The examples are about peduncles, which can be terminal, so position is meaningful. Check that peduncle is not the better part.
An ovule apex can be obtuse.
A lemma tip can be pointed, as in apiculate.
A perigynium can be concavo-convex or plano-convex in cross-section.
The part has a 2-D outline shape, and the examples (ovate, orbicular) are correct.
A megasporophyll scale has a width, given in 'length × width' measurements.
A mericarp apex can be acuminate.
